results.result: The authors developed a novel surgical approach for imaging the lateral cortex (LC) of the inferior colliculus using a microprism-based two-photon microscopy technique. They created a hybrid mouse line (GAD67-GFPx jRGECO1a) to simultaneously visualize GABAergic modules and calcium activity, and modified standard craniotomy procedures to accommodate the deep location and high vascularity of the IC.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C11 describe methodological developments that are well-documented with appropriate citations and figure references. The surgical modifications (C4-C9) address specific technical challenges with empirical solutions (e.g., using agarose instead of saline to reduce motion artifacts). The mouse line generation (C1-C3) follows standard breeding protocols with proper citations to the original transgenic lines.

results.result: Two-photon imaging through the microprism successfully revealed GABAergic modules in the LC in vivo for the first time, with patterns consistent with previous histological reconstructions. The authors validated the microprism location using laser lesions confirmed histologically, and demonstrated that portions of the LC can also be imaged directly from the dorsal surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C19 provide converging evidence for successful LC imaging. The consistency with previous anatomical studies (C13, citations to Chernock et al., 2004; Lesicko Alexandria et al., 2016) validates the approach. Histological confirmation of laser lesions (C14-C15, C18) provides strong spatial validation. The claim of 'first-ever' imaging (C121) appears justified given the technical impossibility stated in C120.

results.result: The GAD67-GFPx jRGECO1a hybrid mice showed non-clustered expression of the calcium indicator jRGECO1a in both DC and LC, with similar expression fractions between regions. The jRGECO1a was expressed exclusively in non-GABAergic neurons, and acoustic stimulation successfully elicited stimulus-dependent calcium signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C24 are supported by statistical analysis (C23: paired t-test, p=0.34, n=10 sections from 2 animals) and figure references. The exclusive expression in non-GABAergic neurons (C24) is demonstrated by lack of GFP co-expression. However, the sample size for the expression comparison (2 animals) is relatively small, though the statistical approach (10 sections) provides reasonable power.

results.result: The LC(microprism) showed inconsistent and fragmentary tonotopic organization with low R² values for regression fits between best tone frequencies and cell locations. Despite this lack of clear tonotopy, cells in modules were tuned to significantly higher frequencies than those in the matrix.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 are supported by quantitative analysis with appropriate statistics (C28: Mann-Whitney test, z=4.03, p=5.6×10⁻⁵, n=215 and 230 cells from 7 animals). The low R² values (C26) and variable regression axes (C27) provide objective evidence for lack of tonotopy. The statistical test for frequency differences between modules and matrix is appropriate and well-powered.

results.result: The DC showed clear tonotopic organization along the rostromedial to caudolateral axis with high R² values, exhibiting a low-frequency bias consistent with previous studies. In contrast, most LC cells were tuned to relatively higher frequencies than DC cells, though about 50% of LC cells showed low-frequency bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 are well-supported with appropriate statistical tests (C34: Mann-Whitney test, z=-11.34, p<0.001) and consistency with multiple previous studies (C32: citations to Ito et al., 2014; Romand and Ehret, 1990; Shen et al., 2003; Stiebler and Ehret, 1985). The quadratic fit providing better R² than linear fit (C30) is appropriately noted and consistent with previous work.

results.result: LC(microprism) cells showed diverse response profiles to pure tones and AM-noise, with significantly higher fractions of noise-selective and non-selective cells compared to tone-selective cells. The matrix had a significantly greater fraction of noise-selective cells than modules, suggesting that matrix neurons are more responsive to spectrally and temporally complex sounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C43 are supported by appropriate statistical analyses (C39: one-way ANOVA, p=1.6×10⁻⁴; C41: Mann-Whitney test, z=-2.32, p=0.02). The inference about matrix neurons being more responsive to complex sounds (C43) is reasonable given the data, though it remains somewhat speculative. Sample sizes appear adequate (7 animals for LC).

results.result: The DC showed significantly higher fractions of noise-selective and non-selective cells than tone-selective cells, with non-selective cells being more abundant than noise-selective cells. Animals showed lower fractions of responsive neurons in LC(microprism) compared to DC, but no significant differences were found between LC(microprism) and LC(dorsal surface), validating the microprism approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by appropriate statistical tests (C44: one-way ANOVA, f(2,9)=86.9, p=1.2×10⁻⁶; C46: two-way ANOVA with appropriate post-hoc tests). The validation comparison (C47) is critical and shows no significant difference in responsiveness between imaging methods (p=0.79), supporting the validity of the microprism approach. Sample sizes are adequate (4-7 animals).

results.result: Matrix regions showed greater proportions of spectrally and temporally modulated cells than modules, with the difference most prominent at sound levels below 70 dB, suggesting lower detection thresholds in matrix cells. LC showed statistically significant higher average SMI and TMI compared to DC, indicating greater sensitivity to spectral and temporal modulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C55 are supported by appropriate two-way ANOVAs with significant main effects and interactions (C49: p=7.1×10⁻⁷ for region; C54: p<0.001 for both SMI and TMI comparisons). The inference about lower detection thresholds (C50) is reasonable given the sound level interaction. However, the general trend of decreasing SMI/TMI with increasing sound level (C53) could benefit from more mechanistic explanation.

results.result: Both modules and matrix of the LC showed auditory and somatosensory responses, with higher fractions of auditory-selective cells overall. However, matrix had more auditory-responsive cells while modules had more somatosensory-responsive cells, consistent with previous anatomical studies showing differential input targeting.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C62 are well-supported by statistical analyses (C60: chi-square test, χ²=33.1, p=3.5×10⁻⁶; C61: χ²=26.0, p=9.3×10⁻⁵) and consistency with previous anatomical work (C57, C62: citation to Lesicko Alexandria et al., 2016). The functional findings align well with known anatomical connectivity patterns, strengthening the conclusions. Sample size is adequate (4 animals).

results.result: Most acoustically responsive cells in the matrix showed onset responses, while offset responses were clustered in modules. A higher fraction of auditory/somatosensory-nonselective cells in modules had offset rather than onset responses. Matrix had more cells with suppressed responses to bimodal stimulation, while modules had more cells with enhanced responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 are supported by appropriate chi-square tests (C63-C64: χ²=120.5, p<0.001; C65: χ²=13.2, p=0.004; C67: χ²=12.9, p=0.04). The statistical tests are appropriate for categorical data. The finding about offset responses in modules (C64) is particularly interesting and well-supported, though the mechanistic interpretation (C131-C132) remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: LC(dorsal surface) imaging showed response profiles consistent with LC(microprism), with both regions having higher percentages of somatosensory responsive cells than DC. The distribution of auditory-selective, onset/offset, and bimodal response properties was similar between imaging approaches, though the ratio of suppressed to enhanced responses in modules may vary with dorsoventral location.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C77 provide important validation of the microprism approach by comparing it to direct dorsal surface imaging. Statistical support is strong (C69: one-way ANOVA, p=0.02; C72: χ²=66.5, p<0.001; C73: χ²=500.2, p<0.001). The suggestion of dorsoventral variation (C77) is appropriately cautious ('may indicate') and represents a reasonable inference from the data, though it would benefit from more systematic testing.

results.result: In awake animals, LC(microprism) showed similar lack of clear tonotopy as in anesthetized animals, with modules tuned to higher frequencies than matrix. DC showed similar tonotopic organization in awake and anesthetized conditions, with a greater proportion of high-frequency cells in the mediodorsal portion. LC had more cells tuned to higher frequencies than DC in awake animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82 demonstrate consistency between awake and anesthetized preparations for key organizational features. Statistical support is adequate (C79: Mann-Whitney test, z=3.8, p=1.0×10⁻⁴; C82: p=1.6×10⁻⁶). The consistency with previous work in awake animals (C81: citation to Wong and Borst, 2019) strengthens the findings. Sample size for awake experiments is smaller (3 animals) but appears sufficient for the main conclusions.

results.result: Both DC and LC of anesthetized animals had higher receptive field widths (RFS) than awake animals, consistent with known effects of ketamine. In both preparations, DC had higher RFS mean than LC, which could be consistent with DC having lower SMI than LC.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are supported by appropriate statistical analysis (C85: Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA, p<0.001) and citation to previous work on ketamine effects (C84: Guo et al., 2012). The connection between RFS and SMI (C86) is appropriately presented as a possibility ('could be consistent') rather than a definitive conclusion. The comparison between awake and anesthetized states provides important context for interpreting the main findings.

results.result: In awake animals, both LC and DC showed higher fractions of noise-selective than tone-selective cells, but the profile of non-selective cells differed from anesthetized animals. Matrix had more spectrally and temporally modulated cells than modules in awake animals, similar to anesthetized animals. However, LC and DC had similar SMI in awake animals, while LC had lower TMI than DC, contrasting with anesthetized findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C93 reveal important differences between awake and anesthetized states. Statistical support is strong (C88: one-way ANOVA, f(2,6)=41.6, p=3.0×10⁻⁴; C90-C91: two-way ANOVAs with p<10⁻⁶; C92-C93: two-way ANOVAs with significant effects). The differences in SMI and TMI between awake and anesthetized states (C92-C93) are particularly important and suggest anesthesia effects on temporal processing, consistent with the discussion of ketamine effects (C138).

results.result: In awake animals, auditory and somatosensory responsive cells were topographically organized across modules and matrix, similar to anesthetized animals, though clustered within pools of nonresponsive cells. Matrix had more auditory responsive cells while modules had more somatosensory responsive cells. Offset cells were rare in awake animals. Modules had higher fractions of suppressed responses than matrix in awake animals, contrasting with anesthetized findings, suggesting arousal state effects on bimodal interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C103 reveal important state-dependent differences in multisensory processing. Statistical support is adequate (C98: χ²=42.5, p=4.4×10⁻⁸; C99: χ²=30.2, p=1.2×10⁻⁶; C102: χ²=31.9, p=5.2×10⁻⁷). The observation about nonresponsive cells (C95-C97) is interesting and appropriately investigated. The inference about arousal state effects (C103) is reasonable but somewhat speculative. The rarity of offset cells in awake animals (C100) contrasts sharply with anesthetized findings and warrants further investigation.

results.result: The microprism approach revealed marked functional differences between LC and DC, and between modules and matrix within the LC. DC displayed tonotopic organization absent in LC; DC neurons were more sound-responsive but both regions preferred complex stimuli; matrix was more responsive to complex stimuli while modules were more responsive to somatosensory stimuli; and bimodal stimulation produced suppression more prominently in matrix. These findings suggest that LC's structural motifs permit functional integration while retaining distinct response properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C108 and C140-C144 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing findings from multiple experiments. These conclusions are well-supported by the extensive data presented in earlier claim groups. The interpretation that structural motifs permit functional integration while retaining distinct properties (C108) is a reasonable synthesis of the anatomical and functional findings, though it remains somewhat inferential.

results.result: The authors provide background on IC organization, noting that it serves as an integration hub with lemniscal (ICC) and non-lemniscal (DC, LC) divisions. The LC contains repeated GABAergic modules embedded in calretinin-positive matrix, with connectivity governed by this organization. Previous work showed multisensory responses in LC with segregated input channels, but the DC has been the only IC region characterized by 2P imaging due to the LC's inaccessible location.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C120 provide essential background and context, all supported by appropriate citations to previous work. These claims establish the rationale for the study and the technical challenge addressed. The citations appear accurate and comprehensive, covering anatomy (C111-C115), connectivity (C116), function (C117-C118), and previous imaging limitations (C119-C120).

results.result: The study demonstrates that modules were more responsive to somatosensory stimulation while matrix was more acoustically responsive with lower detection thresholds for complex sounds. Modules and matrix differentially process spectral and temporal features of acoustic information. No significant differences were found between LC imaging via microprism versus direct dorsal surface imaging, validating the approach, though significant functional differences were observed between LC and DC.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C125, C129-C130 summarize key findings that are well-supported by the detailed experimental results in earlier claim groups. The validation comparison (C129) is critical for establishing the validity of the novel microprism approach. The conclusion that non-lemniscal IC divisions contain distinct platforms for processing different features (C125) is a reasonable synthesis of the findings.

results.result: The authors note that microprism-based 2P microscopy has been successfully used in other brain regions, with previous work showing feasibility for chronic imaging up to 60 days with minimal tissue inflammation. Imaging through a microprism and cover glass appears to have minimal impact on image quality compared to direct 2P imaging.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C128 provide important methodological context, all supported by appropriate citations (Andermann et al., 2013; Heys et al., 2014; Low et al., 2014; Wenzel et al., 2017; Chia and Levene, 2009). These claims establish the precedent for the approach and its feasibility, though the current study was performed acutely rather than chronically.

results.result: The authors discuss potential mechanisms for offset responses and bimodal suppression, noting that offset responses could result from rebound following inhibition termination, suggesting GABAergic cells in modules may play a role in coding sound termination. Combined auditory-somatosensory stimulation generally suppressed auditory responses, most prominently in LC matrix, consistent with previous reports. The origin of these suppressive responses is unclear as auditory-somatosensory interactions occur at multiple levels of the auditory pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C135 involve mechanistic interpretations that are appropriately cautious ('could be', 'may play a role'). The consistency with previous reports (C133-C134) is well-supported by citations. However, the mechanistic claims remain speculative without direct testing of GABAergic cell function (C132) or determination of where suppression originates (C135). These represent reasonable hypotheses for future work rather than established findings.

results.result: The authors discuss ketamine effects on auditory responses, noting that ketamine broadens receptive fields and increases tone-evoked response duration. They suggest ketamine may specifically modulate LC response properties via effects on GABAergic cells, given that GABAergic inhibition contributes to processing temporally modulated signals. This could explain differences in TMI between awake and anesthetized animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C139 provide important context for interpreting differences between awake and anesthetized conditions. The claims about ketamine effects are supported by appropriate citations (C136-C137: Guo et al., 2012; C138-C139: multiple citations). The inference about ketamine specifically affecting LC via GABAergic mechanisms (C138) is reasonable given the data and the known pharmacology, though it remains somewhat speculative without direct pharmacological manipulation.

results.result: The authors developed a novel microprism-based two-photon imaging technique to access the lateral cortex (LC) of the inferior colliculus in vivo. This involved surgical modifications to insert a microprism adjacent to the LC, allowing visualization of GABAergic modules using GAD67-GFP mice crossed with Thy1-jRGECO1a mice for calcium imaging. The technique was validated by comparing microprism imaging with direct dorsal surface imaging and by creating laser lesions that were histologically confirmed.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly praised this methodological achievement. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'provide convincing in vivo evidence' using 'new imaging techniques that provide the first optical access to the lateral cortex in a living animal.' Reviewer 3 describes it as 'a major achievement' requiring 'establishing and refining a challenging surgical procedure' and notes the authors 'validated the accuracy of the microprism technique by directly comparing results obtained with a microprism to data collected using conventional imaging.' Reviewer 4 emphasizes that 'the authors overcame this obstacle by developing methods to implant a microprism' and that they 'validated the accuracy of the microprism technique...finding good correlations between the approaches.'

results.result: The LC showed inconsistent and fragmentary tonotopic organization compared to the DC, which displayed clear tonotopic organization along the rostromedial to caudolateral axis. Despite the lack of consistent tonotopy in the LC, cells in modules were tuned to relatively higher frequencies than those in the matrix. The LC had more cells tuned to higher frequencies compared to the DC. These findings were consistent in both anesthetized and awake animals.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 summarizes that 'both DC and LC of both awake and anaesthetised appears to be more responsive to more complex sounds' and notes 'while both LC and DC appears to have low frequency preferences, this preference for low frequencies is more pronounced in DC.' Reviewer 4 states the authors 'observed that (1) DC displayed tonotopic organization which was not consistently present in the LC.' No reviewer challenges these tonotopic findings.

results.result: Both LC and DC showed preferential responses to spectrally and temporally complex stimuli (amplitude-modulated noise) compared to pure tones. Within the LC, matrix regions were more responsive to spectrally and temporally complex stimuli than modules, with matrix cells having lower detection thresholds for complex sounds. The LC showed higher spectral and temporal modulation indices (SMI and TMI) compared to the DC in anesthetized animals, though this pattern differed in awake animals.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'both DC and LC of both awake and anaesthetised appears to be more responsive to more complex sounds (amplitude modulated noise) compared to pure tones and that under anesthesia the matrix of LC is more modulated by specific frequency and temporal content compared to the gaba'ergic modules in LC.' Reviewer 4 confirms '(2) DC neurons were generally more sound-responsive than LC neurons but that neurons in both regions had preferential responses to spectrally and temporally complex stimuli, (3) matrix regions of the LC were more responsive to spectrally and temporally complex stimuli than modules.'

results.result: Modules were more responsive to somatosensory stimulation than matrix, while matrix regions were more responsive to auditory stimulation. In anesthetized animals, most acoustically responsive cells in the matrix showed onset responses, while cells showing offset responses were clustered in modules. The distribution of auditory and somatosensory responsive cells was consistent with previous anatomical findings showing differential inputs to modules versus matrix. These patterns were observed in both anesthetized and awake animals, though with some differences in the ratio of response types.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'in both awake and anesthetized mice somatosensory inputs are capable of driving responses on its own in the modules of LC, but very little in the matrix.' Reviewer 3 highlights 'the authors find that (a) somatosensory-responses are strongest inside the modules and (b) somatosensory-auditory suppression is stronger in the matrix than in the modules.' Reviewer 4 confirms 'modular neurons were more sensitive to somatosensory stimuli than matrix neurons' and notes 'modular neurons in the anesthetized prep were overall more responsive to auditory stimuli than somatosensory stimuli (albeit with a tendency to have offset responses to sounds).'

results.result: Bimodal auditory-somatosensory stimulation generally suppressed neural responses to auditory stimuli, with this suppression being most prominent in the LC matrix of anesthetized animals. Matrix had a higher fraction of cells with suppressed responses than modules, while modules had a higher fraction of cells with enhanced responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'effects are different in some cases under awake and anesthesia - particularly related to bimodal suppression and enhancement in the modules.' Reviewer 3 states 'somatosensory-auditory suppression is stronger in the matrix than in the modules.' Reviewer 4 confirms 'bimodal, auditory-somatosensory stimuli were more likely to suppress activity in matrix neurons and enhance activity in modular neurons' and summarizes '(4) bimodal stimulation led to suppressive responses that were more prominent in the matrix.'

results.result: Anesthesia (ketamine) affected response properties differently in LC versus DC. Both DC and LC of anesthetized animals had higher receptive field sizes than awake animals. The LC had a higher average of TMIs than the DC in anesthetized animals, but a lower mean of TMIs than the DC in awake animals, suggesting ketamine may specifically modulate LC response properties via effects on GABAergic cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 4 emphasizes this as 'one of the most intriguing results of the present study is the extent to which neural responses in the LC changed in the awake preparation' and notes 'the magnitude and stimulus specificity of the changes caused by anesthesia highlight the extent to which higher-level sensory processing is affected by anesthesia and strongly suggests that future studies of LC function should be conducted in awake animals.' The reviewers accept the ketamine effects as reported, with no challenges to these findings.

results.result: The study revealed marked differences in acoustic response properties between LC and DC, and distinct somatosensory and auditory responses between module and matrix cellular motifs of the LC. Neurons in modules demonstrated primarily offset responses to acoustic stimuli with enhancement in responses to bimodal stimuli, whereas matrix neurons showed onset responses to acoustic stimuli and suppressed responses to bimodal stimulation. The repeated structural motifs of the LC permit functional integration of multimodal inputs while retaining distinct response properties.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states the study 'provides valuable new insights into how multisensory information is processed in the lateral cortex' and that the authors 'provide convincing in vivo evidence that this region contains separate subregions that can be distinguished by their sensory inputs and neurochemical profiles.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'the paper provides new information about how subregions with different inputs and neurochemical profiles in the higher order auditory midbrain process auditory and multisensory information.' Reviewer 4 states 'the results of this study expand our understanding of the functional roles of matrix and module neurons by showing that responses in LC subregions are more complicated than might have been expected based on anatomy alone.'

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the methodological development (C1-C11) and imaging validation (C12-C19, C126-C129). OpenEval provides detailed technical assessment of surgical modifications and histological validation. Peer review emphasizes this as 'a major achievement' with all reviewers praising the novel microprism technique and its validation. Both strongly support these methodological claims.

Both address successful LC imaging claims (C12-C19, C121). OpenEval focuses on anatomical consistency and histological validation, calling it 'first-ever' imaging. Peer review confirms this achievement with Reviewer 1 noting 'first optical access to the lateral cortex in a living animal.' Strong agreement on methodological success.

Both evaluate GCaMP6s expression patterns (C20-C24). OpenEval notes small sample size (2 animals) but adequate statistical power. Peer review does not specifically comment on expression patterns but accepts the overall methodological approach. Implicit agreement through lack of challenge.

Both address tonotopy findings (C25-C28). OpenEval supports lack of tonotopy in LC with appropriate statistics. Peer review (Reviewer 4) confirms 'DC displayed tonotopic organization which was not consistently present in the LC.' Strong agreement on this key finding.

Both evaluate frequency preferences in DC (C29-C34). OpenEval emphasizes statistical support and consistency with previous studies. Peer review (Reviewer 2) notes 'preference for low frequencies is more pronounced in DC.' Agreement on tonotopic organization in DC.

Both address sound complexity responses (C35-C43). OpenEval supports findings with appropriate statistics but notes speculation about matrix neurons. Peer review (Reviewer 2, 4) confirms 'both DC and LC...more responsive to more complex sounds' and 'matrix regions...more responsive to spectrally and temporally complex stimuli.' Strong agreement.

Both evaluate validation comparison between imaging methods (C44-C47). OpenEval emphasizes critical validation showing no significant difference (p=0.79). Peer review (Reviewer 3) confirms authors 'validated the accuracy of the microprism technique...finding good correlations.' Strong agreement on validation.

Both address spectral and temporal modulation findings (C48-C55). OpenEval supports with two-way ANOVAs but notes need for mechanistic explanation. Peer review confirms matrix neurons 'more modulated by specific frequency and temporal content.' Agreement on differential modulation patterns.

Both evaluate somatosensory responses (C56-C62). OpenEval supports with chi-square tests and anatomical consistency. Peer review (Reviewer 2, 3) confirms 'somatosensory inputs...driving responses...in the modules of LC, but very little in the matrix.' Strong agreement on module-matrix differences.

Both address offset responses and temporal patterns (C63-C67). OpenEval supports with chi-square tests but notes speculation. Peer review (Reviewer 4) confirms 'modular neurons...more responsive to auditory stimuli...with a tendency to have offset responses to sounds.' Agreement on offset response patterns.

Both evaluate microprism validation against dorsal imaging (C68-C77). OpenEval provides strong statistical support and notes cautious interpretation of dorsoventral variation. Peer review accepts validation findings without challenge. Agreement on validation approach.

Both address awake vs. anesthetized consistency for organizational features (C78-C82). OpenEval notes smaller sample size (3 animals) but adequate for main conclusions. Peer review confirms findings across both states. Agreement on preserved organizational features.

Both evaluate ketamine effects and anesthesia impacts (C83-C86). OpenEval supports with appropriate statistics and citations. Peer review (Reviewer 4) emphasizes 'one of the most intriguing results' is extent of changes in awake preparation. Strong agreement on anesthesia effects.

Both address awake vs. anesthetized differences in responsiveness and temporal processing (C87-C93). OpenEval provides strong statistical support for SMI/TMI differences. Peer review confirms differences between states. Agreement on state-dependent processing differences.

Both evaluate multisensory integration differences between awake and anesthetized states (C94-C103). OpenEval notes interesting findings about nonresponsive cells and offset cell rarity in awake animals. Peer review confirms bimodal stimulation effects. Agreement on state-dependent multisensory processing.

Both address main conclusions about functional organization (C104-C108, C140-C144). OpenEval synthesizes findings noting some inference. Peer review (all reviewers) confirms study 'provides valuable new insights' and 'expands our understanding of functional roles.' Strong agreement on overall conclusions.

Both evaluate background and rationale claims (C109-C120). OpenEval confirms appropriate citations covering anatomy, connectivity, and previous limitations. Peer review accepts background context without challenge. Agreement on study rationale and context.

Both address summary findings about distinct processing platforms (C122-C125, C129-C130). OpenEval emphasizes validation and reasonable synthesis. Peer review confirms findings about distinct subregions. Agreement on key summary findings.

Both evaluate methodological precedent for microprism approach (C126-C128). OpenEval confirms appropriate citations establishing feasibility. Peer review accepts methodological approach as validated. Agreement on technical precedent.

Both address mechanistic interpretations about suppression and GABAergic function (C131-C135, C133-C134). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN noting appropriate caution but speculation. Peer review (Reviewer 2, 3) confirms suppression findings. Agreement that mechanisms remain somewhat speculative.

Both evaluate ketamine pharmacology and GABAergic mechanisms (C136-C139). OpenEval supports with citations but notes speculation about specific LC effects. Peer review accepts ketamine effects as reported. Agreement on anesthesia impacts with some mechanistic uncertainty.

Overlap on conclusions about distinct processing platforms (C125, C130). OpenEval synthesizes findings as reasonable. Peer review (Reviewer 4) confirms 'responses in LC subregions are more complicated than might have been expected based on anatomy alone.' Agreement on complexity of functional organization.

Overlap on mechanistic interpretations (C131-C132, C135). OpenEval notes speculation about GABAergic mechanisms. Peer review accepts overall conclusions without specifically addressing these mechanistic details. Implicit agreement through lack of challenge.

Overlap on bimodal suppression/enhancement conclusions (C144). OpenEval synthesizes multisensory findings. Peer review (Reviewer 2, 3, 4) confirms 'bimodal suppression and enhancement' differences between modules and matrix. Strong agreement on multisensory integration patterns.
